name.text: Projection of a line onto a plane

questiontext.text:
In the cuboid ABCDEFGH, AB = {@ll@} cm, BC = {@ww@} cm and AE = {@hh@} cm.

(a) The projection of {@lin@} on the plane {@pl@} is

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Find the length of this projection.

[[input:ans2]] cm [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

Give lengths correct to 2 decimal places and angles correct to 1 decimal place. Keep full calculator accuracy until the final answer.

generalfeedback.text:
(a) Drop a perpendicular from each end of {@lin@} to the plane {@pl@}. The projection joins the two feet: it is {@prj@}.

[[if test="two"]]

(b) {@prj@} is a diagonal of a rectangle with sides {@ca@} cm and {@cb@} cm, so \({@prj@}^2 = {@ca@}^2 + {@cb@}^2 = {@S1@}\) and {@prj@} = \(\sqrt{{@S1@}}\) = {@d2(tl)@} cm.

[[else]]

(b) {@prj@} is an edge of the cuboid, so its length is {@tl@} cm.

[[/if]]

questiondescription.text:
Three-Dimensional Geometry: projection of a line onto a plane

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.4: Name the projection of a line on a face of a cuboid and find its length.

Core

This question is adapted from Chapter 34, Section A, question A3 of Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP GCSE Mathematics: Higher 2 for AQA, Edexcel and OCR two-tier GCSE mathematics, Cambridge University Press, 2007: turned round to name the projection of a line on a plane, then find its length; new cases, numbers and wording, randomised, with named feedback.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

feedbackvariables.text: fbk: sublist_indices(DF, lambda([d], is(d[1] = ans1))); fbt: if fbk = [] then "" else if fbk[1] = 2 then sconcat(ans1, " is a perpendicular from an end of ", lin, " to the plane ", pl, ". It joins the line to its projection; the projection itself lies in the plane and joins the feet of the perpendiculars from the two ends of ", lin, ". One foot is an end of ", ans1, ": where is the other?") else if fbk[1] = 4 then sconcat(ans1, " lies in the plane ", pl, ", but drop a perpendicular from each end of ", lin, " to the plane: the two feet are not the two ends of ", ans1, ".") else DF[fbk[1]][2]; nofb: is(fbk = []);

falsefeedback.text:
{@fbt@}

[[if test="nofb"]]

The projection of {@lin@} on {@pl@} joins the feet of the perpendiculars from its two ends.

[[/if]]

truefeedback.text: That is the length of {@lin@} itself. Its projection is shorter: it lies in the plane.
You added the two edges. The projection is the hypotenuse of a right-angled triangle: use Pythagoras.
You found \({@ca@}^2 + {@cb@}^2 = {@S1@}\) but did not take the square root.
That is the length of the perpendicular {@o2@}, not of the projection.
Your answer is close but not accurate to 2 decimal places. Keep full calculator accuracy until the end (store values, or keep the square root), then round the length once.

falsefeedback.text: The projection lies in the plane {@pl@}, so it is an edge or a diagonal of that face. Your length squared is {@d2(sq2)@}. For a diagonal that should be the sum of the squares of the two edges of the face; an edge can be read from the dimensions. Which is it here?

qtest.description: A perpendicular; edges added (NA on edge entries)
The other diagonal; no square root (NA on edge entries)
